results.name: below_min_vs_above_max_extension
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples, yes rate for targets 1-15 below the smallest example minus yes rate for targets 1-15 above the largest example; observed above the null means people extend downward more readily than the model's symmetric intervals/rules predict (below = they extend upward more).
results.code:
# name: below_min_vs_above_max_extension
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples, yes rate for targets 1-15 below the smallest example minus yes rate for targets 1-15 above the largest example; observed above the null means people extend downward more readily than the model's symmetric intervals/rules predict (below = they extend upward more).
def test_statistic(df):
    exm = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(exm, axis=1)
    hi = np.nanmax(exm, axis=1)
    n = (~np.isnan(exm)).sum(axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    a = (n >= 2) & (t < lo) & (lo - t <= 15)
    b = (n >= 2) & (t > hi) & (t - hi <= 15)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: shared_digit_far_target_contrast
results.description: For non-example targets more than 15 away from every example, yes rate when the target shares at least one decimal digit with some example minus yes rate when it shares none; observed above the null means people use loose digit similarity beyond what the model's all-examples-contain-digit rules produce (below = less digit-driven than the model).
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_far_target_contrast
# description: For non-example targets more than 15 away from every example, yes rate when the target shares at least one decimal digit with some example minus yes rate when it shares none; observed above the null means people use loose digit similarity beyond what the model's all-examples-contain-digit rules produce (below = less digit-driven than the model).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    uniq = sets.unique()
    ex_map = {s: np.array([int(x) for x in s.split(",")]) for s in uniq}
    mind = np.empty(len(df)); share = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
    ss = sets.to_numpy()
    tdig = [set(str(v)) for v in range(101)]
    for s in uniq:
        idx = np.where(ss == s)[0]
        ex = ex_map[s]
        tt = t[idx]
        mind[idx] = np.abs(tt[:, None] - ex[None, :]).min(axis=1)
        digs = set("".join(str(e) for e in ex))
        lut = np.array([len(tdig[v] & digs) > 0 for v in range(101)])
        share[idx] = lut[tt]
    far = mind > 15
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    a, b = far & share, far & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples and non-example targets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the last-shown example (and more than 10 from the first) minus yes rate for targets within 10 of the first-shown example (and more than 10 from the last); the model ignores presentation order, so observed above the null means a recency effect in generalization (below = primacy).
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples and non-example targets, yes rate for targets within 10 of the last-shown example (and more than 10 from the first) minus yes rate for targets within 10 of the first-shown example (and more than 10 from the last); the model ignores presentation order, so observed above the null means a recency effect in generalization (below = primacy).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    parts = sets.str.split(",")
    first = parts.str[0].astype(int).to_numpy()
    last = parts.str[-1].astype(int).to_numpy()
    n = parts.str.len().to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    exm = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    inset = (exm == df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    df1 = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~inset
    a = base & (dl <= 10) & (df1 > 10)
    b = base & (df1 <= 10) & (dl > 10)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: set_level_yes_rate_sd
results.description: SD across example sets (with at least 10 non-example-target trials) of each set's yes rate on non-example targets; observed above the null means sets differ in how broadly people generalize more than the model captures (model too homogeneous across sets), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set differences.
results.code:
# name: set_level_yes_rate_sd
# description: SD across example sets (with at least 10 non-example-target trials) of each set's yes rate on non-example targets; observed above the null means sets differ in how broadly people generalize more than the model captures (model too homogeneous across sets), below means the model exaggerates set-to-set differences.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    exm = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    inset = (exm == df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    sub = df[~inset]
    g = sub.groupby(sets[~inset])["rating"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 10]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())

results.name: cell_unanimity_fraction
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells with at least 5 responses whose responses are all identical (all yes or all no); observed above the null means people respond more deterministically/consistently per stimulus than the model's intermediate posterior probabilities imply (below = people are more variable than the model).

results.name: ext_multiple_smaller_factor_yes
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all multiples of some m in 13..50 (largest such m), yes rate for non-example targets that are not multiples of m but are multiples of a familiar factor f in 3..12 that divides every example; observed above the null means the model's extended multiples-of-13..50 rules over-suppress generalization to the smaller familiar factor (below = people suppress even more).

results.name: round_number_target_bias
results.description: Among sets not consisting entirely of multiples of 5, yes rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate for other non-example targets; observed above the null means people favour round-number targets beyond what the model's rules predict (below = they disfavour them).
results.code:
# name: round_number_target_bias
# description: Among sets not consisting entirely of multiples of 5, yes rate for non-example targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes rate for other non-example targets; observed above the null means people favour round-number targets beyond what the model's rules predict (below = they disfavour them).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    m5 = {s: all(int(x) % 5 == 0 for x in s.split(",")) for s in sets.unique()}
    keep = ~sets.map(m5).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    exm = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    inset = (exm == df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    base = keep & ~inset
    a = base & (t % 10 == 0)
    b = base & (t % 10 != 0)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: prime_set_prime_vs_odd_composite
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all primes, yes rate for non-example prime targets minus yes rate for odd composite targets; observed above the null means people use the prime concept more sharply than the model's prime-vs-odd weighting implies (below = people treat all-prime sets as merely odd more than the model does).
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_vs_odd_composite
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all primes, yes rate for non-example prime targets minus yes rate for odd composite targets; observed above the null means people use the prime concept more sharply than the model's prime-vs-odd weighting implies (below = people treat all-prime sets as merely odd more than the model does).
def test_statistic(df):
    primes = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    isp = np.array([v in primes for v in range(101)])
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    ok = {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        ok[s] = len(ex) >= 2 and all(e in primes for e in ex)
    keep = sets.map(ok).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    exm = sets.str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    inset = (exm == df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    base = keep & ~inset
    a = base & isp[t]
    b = base & ~isp[t] & (t % 2 == 1) & (t > 1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
